questions.question: What is the aim of the Layered Architecture experiment?
questions.answer: To implement a Student Management System using the layered (N-tier) architecture, separating the presentation, business logic and data access layers

questions.question: How does layered architecture organise an application?
questions.answer: It divides the application into horizontal layers; each layer has one responsibility and may only talk to the layer directly below it

questions.question: Why doesn't a change in one layer affect the whole layered system?
questions.answer: Because every layer has one responsibility and only talks to the layer directly below it, so changes don't ripple through the system

questions.question: What advantages of layered architecture are given in the practical file?
questions.answer: Separation of concerns, easy testing, and any layer can be replaced (e.g. SQLite by MySQL) without touching the others

What does a load balancer do?
questions.answer: It sits in front of several servers and spreads client requests among them to improve throughput and availability

questions.question: How does the Round-Robin algorithm assign requests?
questions.answer: In a fixed circular order (S1, S2, S3, S1, ...)

questions.question: What is the limitation of plain Round-Robin load balancing?
questions.answer: It ignores the current load and capacity of a server (weighted variants fix this)

questions.question: How does the load balancer avoid sending requests to a failed server?
questions.answer: It checks a health flag and skips unhealthy servers, using the next healthy one

What is the aim of the API rate limiter experiment?
questions.answer: To implement an API rate limiter using the Token Bucket algorithm that limits the number of requests per client

questions.question: Why is rate limiting used?
questions.answer: It protects a service from overload and abuse by restricting how many requests a client may send in a period

questions.question: What HTTP status code rejects requests above the rate limit?
questions.answer: 429 (Too Many Requests)

questions.question: How does the Token Bucket algorithm work?
questions.answer: A bucket holds up to 'capacity' tokens and is refilled at a fixed rate; each request consumes one token

questions.question: How large a burst of requests does the token bucket allow?
questions.answer: Up to 'capacity' requests; after that requests are accepted only as fast as tokens are refilled

questions.question: Why does the rate limiter keep one bucket per client?
questions.answer: So a heavy client does not affect the others

questions.question: What is the file name of the rate limiter program?
questions.answer: rateLimiter.js

questions.question: What capacity and refill rate does the RateLimiter demo use?

questions.question: How is the retry-after time calculated by the rate limiter?
questions.answer: (1 - tokens) / refillRate seconds

questions.question: How many tokens were left after client B's first request?
How many of client A's requests were accepted after waiting 3 seconds?
questions.answer: 3 (the 4th got 429)

questions.question: What does the conclusion of the rate limiter experiment say?
questions.answer: It accepted a burst of five requests, rejected extra ones with 429, tracked clients separately and allowed requests again once tokens refilled

questions.question: What is the aim of the circuit breaker experiment?
questions.answer: To implement the Circuit Breaker pattern with a retry mechanism using exponential back-off so calls to an unreliable service are fault tolerant

questions.question: Why does a circuit breaker stop calls to a failing service?
questions.answer: So the system fails fast and the service gets time to recover

questions.question: What are the three states of a circuit breaker?
questions.answer: CLOSED, OPEN and HALF-OPEN

questions.question: What happens in the HALF-OPEN state?
questions.answer: One trial call is allowed; if it succeeds the circuit closes, otherwise it opens again

questions.question: When does a closed circuit become open?
questions.answer: When the counted failures reach the threshold

questions.question: What retry delays does the exponential back-off produce?
questions.answer: 0.1 s, 0.2 s, 0.4 s ... (base delay × 2^attempt)

questions.question: What are the default failure threshold and recovery timeout of the CircuitBreaker class?
questions.answer: Failure threshold 3 and recovery timeout 2.0 seconds

questions.question: What error is thrown when the circuit is open?
questions.answer: CircuitOpenError: circuit OPEN - call blocked

questions.question: Why doesn't the retry wrapper retry a CircuitOpenError?
questions.answer: There is no point retrying while the circuit is open, so it is re-thrown at once

questions.question: What does FlakyService do?
questions.answer: It fails for the first failFirst calls (service unavailable) and then returns 200 OK

questions.question: How many attempts did demo 1 need before the flaky service returned 200 OK?
questions.answer: 3 (two failures, then success)

questions.question: What recovery timeout is used for the breaker in demo 2?
questions.answer: 1.5 seconds

questions.question: What state transitions happened at call 4 in the circuit breaker demo?
questions.answer: OPEN -> HALF_OPEN, then HALF_OPEN -> CLOSED

questions.question: What happened to calls 2 and 3 in the circuit breaker demo?
questions.answer: They failed immediately with circuit OPEN - call blocked

What does Engineering Economics deal with?
questions.answer: The application of economic principles and techniques to engineering decision-making

questions.question: What are the objectives of Engineering Economics?
questions.answer: Minimize cost, maximize profit, efficient utilization of resources, economic evaluation of alternatives, support managerial decisions

questions.question: What is the scope of Engineering Economics?
questions.answer: Production planning, project evaluation, inventory control, replacement decisions, make-or-buy decisions, value engineering and cost analysis

questions.question: What is a fixed cost?
questions.answer: A cost that does not change with the level of production

questions.question: Give examples of fixed costs from the revision notes.
questions.answer: Rent, salary, insurance

questions.question: What is a variable cost?
questions.answer: A cost that changes with production volume (e.g. raw material, power)

questions.question: What is a semi-variable cost?
questions.answer: A cost that contains both fixed and variable components

questions.question: What is a sunk cost?
questions.answer: A past cost that cannot be recovered

questions.question: What is opportunity cost?
questions.answer: The benefit sacrificed by selecting one alternative over another

questions.question: What is the break-even point?
questions.answer: The point where Total Revenue = Total Cost

questions.question: What is the formula for contribution per unit?
questions.answer: Contribution = Selling Price – Variable Cost

questions.question: How is the break-even quantity calculated?
questions.answer: BEP = Fixed Cost / Contribution per unit

questions.question: What is the formula for break-even sales value?
questions.answer: BEP Sales = Fixed Cost / P/V Ratio

questions.question: How is the P/V ratio calculated?
questions.answer: P/V Ratio = Contribution / Sales × 100

questions.question: What is the margin of safety formula?
questions.answer: MOS = Actual Sales – Break-even Sales

questions.question: How is profit computed from contribution?
questions.answer: Profit = Contribution – Fixed Cost

questions.question: How is demand defined in the notes?
questions.answer: The quantity of a commodity consumers are willing to buy at a given price

questions.question: What does the law of demand say about price and quantity?
questions.answer: When price increases demand decreases and vice versa: a negative relationship between price and quantity demanded

questions.question: What factors affect demand?
questions.answer: Price, income, population, taste and preference, availability of substitutes

questions.question: What does the law of supply state?
questions.answer: When price increases, supply increases

questions.question: What factors affect supply?
questions.answer: Production cost, technology, taxation, government policy

questions.question: What is the difference between technical and economic efficiency?
questions.answer: Technical efficiency is producing maximum output from given resources; economic efficiency is producing the desired output at minimum possible cost

questions.question: What is the decision criterion for technical versus economic efficiency?
questions.answer: Higher productivity for technical efficiency; lower total cost for economic efficiency

questions.question: In the machine example, why may the 800-unit machine be economically more efficient?
questions.answer: Because it may produce its 800 units at significantly lower cost, even though the 1,000-unit machine is technically more efficient

questions.question: Why is elementary economic analysis needed?
questions.answer: For comparing alternatives before selecting the best engineering decision

questions.question: What are the applications of elementary economic analysis?
questions.answer: Material selection, design selection, process planning, equipment selection, transportation decisions

questions.question: On what basis are alternative materials compared?
questions.answer: Material cost, processing cost, transportation cost, weight and operating cost

questions.question: What is economic advantage in material selection?
questions.answer: The difference in total cost between alternatives

questions.question: What are the steps in process planning?
questions.answer: Analyze drawing, identify operations, select machines, determine process sequence, estimate cost

questions.question: What is process modification?
questions.answer: Modifying an existing process to reduce production cost

questions.question: How is total processing cost calculated?
questions.answer: Cost = Machine Hour Rate × Processing Time

questions.question: What is the time value of money?
questions.answer: The principle that money available today is worth more than the same amount received in the future

questions.question: Why does money have time value?
questions.answer: Earning capacity, inflation, risk and uncertainty, and preference for present consumption

questions.question: What is the simple interest formula?
questions.answer: I = P × n × i, and F = P(1 + ni)

questions.question: What is the compound interest formula for future amount?
questions.answer: F = P(1 + i)^n

questions.answer: Identify cash flows, convert to present worth, compare alternatives, select highest PW

questions.question: What advantages of the present worth method are listed?
questions.answer: Considers time value of money, easy comparison of projects, widely used

questions.question: How does the future worth method treat cash flows?
questions.answer: All cash flows are converted to future value at the end of project life

questions.question: What is the future worth formula?
questions.answer: FW = Future worth of benefits – Future worth of costs

questions.question: What advantages does the future worth method have?
questions.answer: Useful for long-term planning and easy understanding of the accumulated amount

questions.question: What does the annual equivalent method do?
questions.answer: Converts all cash flows into an equivalent annual amount

questions.question: How is annual equivalent cost calculated?
questions.answer: AEC = Capital Recovery + Annual Operating Cost

questions.question: Which alternative is preferred under the annual equivalent method for cost alternatives?
questions.answer: The one with minimum AEC (maximum annual equivalent for revenue alternatives)

questions.question: Why is the annual equivalent method suitable for alternatives with different lives?
questions.answer: It reduces each alternative to an equivalent annual amount, which allows easy annual comparison

questions.question: What is the internal rate of return?
questions.answer: The interest rate at which the present worth of benefits equals the present worth of costs, i.e. NPW = 0

questions.answer: When IRR > MARR; reject when IRR < MARR

questions.answer: Minimum Attractive Rate of Return

questions.question: What is replacement analysis?
questions.answer: The economic evaluation of whether an existing asset should be retained or replaced with a new one

questions.question: What are the types of deterioration?
questions.answer: Physical deterioration (wear and tear) and functional/technological obsolescence

questions.question: What are the defender and the challenger in replacement analysis?
questions.answer: The defender is the existing asset; the challenger is the proposed replacement

questions.question: When should a machine be replaced according to the replacement procedure?
questions.answer: When the annual equivalent cost of the new machine is lower than that of the old one

questions.question: What is depreciation?
questions.answer: The gradual decrease in the value of an asset over time due to wear and tear, age, usage, obsolescence or other factors

questions.question: What is the straight line depreciation formula?
questions.answer: Depreciation = (First Cost – Salvage Value) / Life

questions.question: How is book value calculated?
questions.answer: BV = First Cost – Accumulated Depreciation

questions.question: How is depreciation calculated under the declining balance method?
questions.answer: Depreciation = Book Value × Depreciation Rate

questions.question: What is the sum of years digits depreciation formula?
questions.answer: Depreciation = Remaining Life / Sum of Digits × (Cost – Salvage)

questions.question: Why is depreciation important?
questions.answer: Tax calculation, profit estimation, replacement planning

questions.answer: When B/C > 1; a higher B/C is preferred

questions.answer: Tangible benefits are direct monetary benefits; intangible benefits are social or environmental

questions.question: How is inflation defined in the notes?
questions.answer: A continuous increase in the general price level

questions.answer: (1 + Market Rate) = (1 + Real Rate)(1 + Inflation Rate)

questions.answer: The interest rate excluding inflation (the market rate includes it)

questions.question: What is inventory?
questions.answer: Stock of materials kept for future use

questions.question: What are the objectives of inventory control?
questions.answer: Avoid shortage, reduce inventory cost, smooth production

questions.question: What are the types of inventory costs?
questions.answer: Ordering cost, carrying cost and shortage cost

questions.question: What is carrying cost?
questions.answer: The cost of storing inventory

questions.question: What is a make-or-buy decision?

questions.question: What factors affect the make-or-buy decision?

questions.question: What is the break-even quantity formula for make or buy?

questions.question: What are the phases of project management?

questions.question: What does the scheduling phase of a project determine?
questions.answer: The start and end times of each activity, summarized in a time chart/Gantt chart

questions.question: When is CPM used instead of PERT?
questions.answer: CPM is used when activity times are certain; PERT when they are uncertain

questions.answer: Program Evaluation Review Technique

questions.question: What is the critical path?
questions.answer: The longest path in the project network; its activities have zero slack

questions.question: How is slack time calculated?
questions.answer: Slack = LFT – EFT (difference between latest and earliest event time)

questions.answer: Network flows left to right, no loops, use arrows for directions

questions.question: What is value analysis?
questions.answer: A systematic approach to improve the value of a product by eliminating unnecessary costs without reducing quality, performance, reliability or functionality
